opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it really started from a fairly simple observation. We train enormous numbers of neural networks — in our group, across the community, on model zoos and hubs — and once training is done, we basically throw away everything except maybe the final checkpoint and a validation score. But those weights are the actual artifact of learning. They encode everything the model has picked up about the data, the task, the optimization trajectory. And yet we almost never treat the weights themselves as a data modality.

So the question became: what if we look at populations of trained models and ask whether the weights, on their own, carry structure we can learn from? Early on we tried more hand-crafted approaches, computing statistics over the weights, things like means, variances, norms per layer, and feeding those into simple predictors. And surprisingly, that already told you a lot. You could predict test accuracy, or roughly where a model was in training, or which hyperparameters were used, just from those weight statistics.

But that's the classic situation where you've designed features by hand, and the deep learning lesson over the last decade has been that if you have enough data, learned representations usually beat engineered ones. So the natural next step was to go end-to-end: build model zoos, large, systematically generated collections of trained networks, and then train a representation learner directly on the weights. We used self-supervised approaches, things like hyper-representations with transformer-style encoders over weight tokens, with augmentations that respect the symmetries of neural networks, such as permutation symmetries of neurons, so the representation doesn't get confused by equivalent models that just look different in weight space.

What's exciting is that once you have that learned embedding space, it becomes a kind of lens into the models. You can predict properties like generalization or robustness, and you can even go the other way, generating new weights by sampling from that space, which is useful for initialization or transfer. So the end-to-end framing came from wanting to stop guessing which aspects of the weights matter and let the data, here a population of models, tell us.

r001.rationale: The response describes computing hand-crafted weight statistics, then motivates end-to-end learning as a way to let data determine which weight features matter.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning representations directly from weights, but does not propose autoencoding them or explicitly describe a lower-dimensional representation of the network population.

r003.rationale: It says weights encode learned information and that statistics can predict hyperparameters, but does not hypothesize that the learned weight manifold encodes factors that generated the networks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. It actually came out of frustration more than a grand plan. In my group at the University of St. Gallen we train an enormous number of neural networks, and at some point I realized we treat the weights as a black box in a way we'd never accept for any other data modality. If you give me an image or a time series, I have a whole toolbox to look at it, cluster it, compare it. But if you give me a trained network, the most anyone does is look at the loss curve and maybe a histogram of the parameters.

So the question we asked ourselves was almost naive: what if we treat the weights themselves as the data? Can you look at a weight matrix and say something about what happened to this model, how it was trained, how it will behave on new data, whether it was poisoned, how good it is, without ever running it on inputs?

The first attempts were very hand-crafted. We computed statistics, norms, eigenvalue spectra, things like that, and fed them to a classifier. And it worked to some degree, but it felt like the feature-engineering era of computer vision all over again. I had lived through that transition, from SIFT features to convolutional networks learning their own representations, and the lesson was pretty clear: if you have enough data, let the model discover the structure rather than imposing your own priors on it.

The problem was we didn't have enough data. There were no large collections of trained networks lying around. So we built them. We call them model zoos, thousands of small networks trained on the same task with controlled variation in hyperparameters, seeds, initializations, and so on. Once we had that, end-to-end learning became the natural step. We could train a second network, essentially an encoder on top of the weights, and learn a representation of the weight space directly, with self-supervision, without me telling it which statistics matter.

And what was striking is that the learned representations captured properties we hadn't explicitly asked for. You could predict test accuracy, generalization gap, which optimizer was used, even the training epoch, from the embedding alone. That told us there is real, recoverable structure in weight space, and that we should stop hand-designing the lens and let the data tell us how to look.

r001.rationale: The response describes hand-crafted weight statistics fed to a classifier, then explains that it wanted the model to learn weight structure directly instead of relying on designed features.

r002.rationale: It describes an encoder that learns weight embeddings, but does not propose autoencoding the weights.

r003.rationale: It asks whether weights reveal how a model was trained and reports that embeddings predict the optimizer and training epoch, showing that learned representations may encode factors of the training process.

astra-6.text:
The starting point was a question: once we’ve trained a neural network, can we learn something from its weights directly? We usually try to understand a network by looking at its predictions or its activations for particular inputs. But the weights are where the result of training is stored, so it seemed natural to ask whether we could analyze that representation itself.

The difficulty is that individual weights don’t have an obvious meaning in isolation. Their role depends on how they interact with the rest of the network. So rather than deciding beforehand which statistics would be useful, we could treat the weights as data and learn a representation of them end to end.

That shifts the problem: we’re using learning to study the products of learning. The hope is that the representation captures meaningful differences between networks—how they behave, for example—and gives us a way to investigate what’s encoded in their weights. It doesn’t automatically make every weight interpretable, but it gives us a starting point for understanding the network as a whole.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts analyzing weights with examining predictions or activations and says to learn a representation end to end, but it does not identify prior reliance on handcrafted features extracted from weights as the motivation.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning a representation of weights, but does not specify autoencoding or a lower-dimensional representation of a population of networks.

r003.rationale: It suggests the representation could capture differences between networks and help investigate what weights encode, but does not hypothesize that the weight manifold encodes generating factors such as training data or hyperparameters.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the starting point was the question of what a neural network actually learns. We train these models, and much of what they learn is stored in the weights, but looking at an individual weight tells you very little. Its meaning depends on how it interacts with the rest of the network.

So we turned the question around: could we learn something about those weights using another neural network? Instead of manually defining what to measure, we could treat the weights of a trained model as data and learn a representation of them end to end. The hope is that this representation captures meaningful differences between models and gives us a way to investigate their behavior. That doesn’t automatically make every weight interpretable, but it gives us another way to study what the network has learned.

r001.rationale: It contrasts end-to-end learning with manually defining what to measure, but does not identify prior use of handcrafted features extracted from weights.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning a representation of weights, but does not specify autoencoding, a lower-dimensional representation, or a population of networks.

r003.rationale: It says the representation may capture differences between models, but does not hypothesize that the weight manifold encodes generating factors such as training data or hyperparameters.
